extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funding agency staff, policymakers and methodologists interested in peer review of grant applications
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review of comparative studies of grant-giving peer review processes to assess their effects on the identification of high-quality proposals and on the eventual quality of funded research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes of grant-giving peer review (grouping of interventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The review groups peer-review processes as: different ways of screening, assigning or masking submissions; different ways of eliciting internal or external opinions; different decision making procedures (group or single person); different types of feedback to author(s) and subsequent revision of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These process categories define the interventions that comparative studies should examine. The review uses these groupings to classify included studies and to identify gaps where experimental evidence is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of funded research (primary outcome measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of the funded research, however measured, including importance, relevance, usefulness, soundness of methods, soundness of ethics, completeness and accuracy of funded research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review highlights these dimensions as the meaningful end outcomes to assess the effect of peer review procedures and calls for experimental studies measuring these directly; no included studies directly assessed these outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility/inclusion criteria for studies assessing peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective or retrospective comparative studies with two or more comparison groups (random or other methods, including historical comparisons) assessing different interventions or an intervention against 'doing nothing'; only original research proposals and quality outcome measures were considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the methodological scope for studies to be considered informative about peer review effects; used to exclude descriptive or opinion pieces without comparative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening procedures (triage vs detailed/full review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different ways of screening submissions (i.e. carrying out a preliminary assessment of the submission) such as simplified assessment/triage models versus standard, detailed procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative studies (Russel 1983; Vener 1993) suggest simplified screening or five-member triage models appear to have little effect on final ratings or to rarely eliminate highly competitive applications, but study quality and generalisability are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masking / blinding of submissions (open vs blinded review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different ways of masking submissions (i.e. concealing the identity and background of the authors and/or the assessors); comparison of open (sighted) versus blinded reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective evidence (Lee 2000) indicates sighted reviewers behave differently and their assessments can be affected by applicant/institution rank, professional age and academic recognition—indicating potential bias in open review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of reviewers (methods for choosing assessors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different ways of assigning submissions (i.e. choosing and assigning assessors to the submission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study designs comparing assignment mechanisms examine whether who is chosen to review affects scores and funding decisions; the review notes wide variability in assignment practice across settings and limited generalisable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliciting internal versus external opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different ways of eliciting internal opinions (opinions from those within the grant-giving organisation) versus external opinions (those outside the organisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies (e.g. Hodgson 1995) found internal reviewer scores were more closely correlated with final committee decisions than external reviewers' scores; implications for fairness and reliability should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-making procedures (committee vs individual; composition and process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different (group or single person) decision making procedures (i.e. deciding whether to fund the submission), including full committees versus small triage panels or different institutional review bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons of different decision-making systems produced conflicting results (Das 1985; Hodgson; Cole 1981), suggesting outcomes can depend heavily on setting, group composition and selection biases; no clear superiority of a particular model was established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback to applicants and subsequent revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of feedback to author(s) and subsequent revision of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a category of intervention to be studied; the review notes a lack of comparative evidence on whether the nature or amount of feedback and opportunity to revise improves the quality of funded research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific reviewer assessment criteria (items reviewers rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual items used by reviewers to assess proposals, e.g. clarity of goal, originality, methodology, desirability of outcomes, qualification of applicants, research team, budget, duration, training (Lee 2000); and parameters such as knowledge of subject, experience, objectives, research plan, data processing, innovation, adequacy, institution and age (Wiener 1977).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review documents a wide range of criteria used in practice; Hartmann (1990) classified review comments into 11 criteria categories. The heterogeneity of criteria complicates comparisons and may affect reliability and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring/rating scale design and granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties of scoring scales used in peer review (e.g. different rating intervals: 0.5 versus 0.1 point intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Green 1989 found little effect of finer-grained (0.1) versus coarser (0.5) rating intervals on final assessments; scale design alone may not substantially change outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-reviewer agreement and reliability metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement of results of peer review processes as an outcome measure; methods include standard error of the mean, coefficient of variance, weighted priority scores, and Cohen's kappa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many included studies reported high inter-reviewer agreement on some aspects (e.g. theoretical/methodological quality, appropriateness of budget) and greater agreement for high-priority applications, but measurement methods varied and some choices (e.g. use of coefficient of variance) were criticised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential biases affecting peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported or investigated biases including gender, age, institution, 'cronyism', discipline, professional age, academic recognition and personal relationships between applicant and reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence is mixed: some studies report biases (Wenneras 1997), others do not. The review cautions that many claims about bias are based on personal experience; rigorous comparative research is needed to quantify and mitigate such biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological quality assessment criteria for studies of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used to assess the methodological quality of included studies: for randomized studies — randomisation, generation of allocation sequence, allocation concealment, blinding; for cohort studies — Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; for other designs — methodological assessment grids (e.g., NHS Centre for Review and Dissemination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review applied these quality assessment tools and categorized study quality as adequate/possible adequate/inadequate; many included studies were retrospective with limitations reducing generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for practice and research (evaluation, transparency, innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt reviewing practices aimed to evaluate and control potentially negative effects of peer review; attempts to improve efficiency and transparency of the process and actions encouraging innovative ideas should be implemented and evaluated; organise properly designed experimental studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors conclude experimental studies assessing effects of peer review on the defined quality outcomes are urgently needed. Meanwhile, implement practices to monitor and limit potential negative effects (bias, inefficiency) and evaluate reforms empirically.
